symptoms: Olive-green to brown spots on leaves that later turn dark and velvety
Scabby, corky lesions on fruit that may crack
Premature leaf yellowing and drop in severe cases
Fruit may become deformed and unmarketable
Apple___Apple_scab.cause: Fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. Favoured by cool, wet weather in spring.
Apple___Apple_scab.treatment: Remove and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Prune to improve air circulation. Apply recommended fungicides at green tip, pink bud and petal fall stages following the local spray schedule of Himachal Pradesh Horticulture Department / Dr Y.S. Parmar University. pesticides.dosage: 600 g per 200 L water (as per 2024 HP spray schedule)

pesticides.name: Captan
pesticides.dosage: 600 g per 200 L water (Captan) or as per label
pesticides.application: Foliar spray; avoid before/after oil sprays for 15 days.
pesticides.source: Department of Horticulture, Himachal Pradesh & Dr Y.S. Parmar University of Horticulture and Forestry, 2024 spray schedule

Apple___Apple_scab.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance. Balanced nutrition helps plant recovery.
prevention: Rake and destroy fallen leaves to reduce overwintering inoculum
Plant scab-resistant varieties where available
Prune canopy for better air flow and light penetration
Follow recommended spray schedule based on tree phenology and weather

Maintain tree vigour through proper nutrition and irrigation

Maintain good orchard sanitation
Follow timely fungicide applications based on weather

Plant less susceptible varieties if available
Remove severely infected shoots

Destroy or deeply bury crop residue

Grape___Black_rot.treatment: Remove and destroy all mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning. Improve air circulation. Apply protectant fungicides (copper or mancozeb-based) starting from early shoot growth according to ICAR-NRCG guidelines.
Grape___Black_rot.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance. Avoid excess nitrogen.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).treatment: No curative chemical treatment is fully effective once established. Remove and destroy severely affected vines. Protect pruning wounds. Maintain vine health through balanced nutrition and irrigation. Consult local grape pathologist for latest recommendations.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance. Balanced nutrition and avoidance of stress help reduce severity.
prevention: Protect pruning wounds with approved wound sealants or fungicides
Prune in dry weather and avoid large cuts when possible
Remove and burn infected wood
Maintain good vine vigour and avoid water stress
Use healthy planting material

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: Bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri).
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).treatment: There is no curative treatment. Remove and destroy infected trees promptly. Control the psyllid vector with recommended insecticides. Use only disease-free planting material produced through shoot-tip grafting or indexed mother plants (ICAR-CCRI protocol). Apply micronutrients (Zn, Mn, B) to prolong productive life of mildly affected trees.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).fertilizer: Foliar sprays of zinc sulphate + manganese sulphate + boric acid as recommended by ICAR-CCRI can help manage symptoms and improve yield of infected trees. Consult local citrus specialist for exact doses and timing.
prevention: Use only certified disease-free planting material from indexed mother blocks
Control Asian citrus psyllid rigorously, especially during flush periods
Remove and destroy symptomatic trees as soon as detected
Maintain orchard hygiene and avoid movement of infected material
Follow ICAR-Central Citrus Research Institute advisories

Avoid overhead irrigation
Plant resistant varieties

Space plants properly

Black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) visible in the centre of spots
Lower leaves affected first; progressive defoliation
Fruit is rarely directly infected
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici. Survives on crop residue and weeds. Spread by rain splash.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Remove lower infected leaves. Practise crop rotation. Apply mancozeb or other protectant fungicides at first symptom. Improve air circulation.

pesticides.name: Mancozeb 75% WP
pesticides.dosage: 600–800 g in 300 L water per acre
pesticides.application: Foliar spray at first appearance of symptoms.
pesticides.source: PPQS AESA based IPM – Tomato

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance.

Remove and destroy infected plant debris

Avoid working in wet fields
Use disease-free transplants

symptoms: Fine stippling (tiny yellow/white spots) on upper leaf surface
Leaves become bronzed or yellowish and may dry
Fine webbing on underside of leaves in heavy infestation
Reduced plant vigour and fruit quality
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Pest (arachnid) – Tetranychus urticae (two-spotted spider mite). Thrives in hot, dry conditions. Multiplies rapidly.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment: Monitor regularly. Use miticides (fenazaquin, spiromesifen) when populations exceed threshold. Encourage natural enemies. Avoid excessive nitrogen and dusty conditions. Overhead irrigation can help suppress mites temporarily.

pesticides.name: Fenazaquin 10% EC
pesticides.dosage: 500 ml in 200 L water per acre (or ~2.5 ml/L)
pesticides.application: Foliar spray, ensuring good coverage of undersides of leaves.

pesticides.name: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC
pesticides.dosage: 250 ml in 200 L water per acre (or ~1.25 ml/L)
pesticides.application: Foliar spray targeting undersides of leaves.

Lesions may have a yellow halo
Fruit can develop dark, sunken spots
Defoliation in severe cases
Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Favoured by warm, humid conditions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.treatment: Improve air circulation. Remove infected lower leaves. Apply protectant fungicides (mancozeb, chlorothalonil) or registered systemic products at first symptom. Practise crop rotation.
Tomato___Target_Spot.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance.
prevention: Crop rotation with non-host crops
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
Stake plants and maintain good spacing
Avoid overhead irrigation when possible
Use healthy transplants

symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaves
Leaves become small, thick and leathery
Severe stunting of plants
Reduced or no fruit set; flowers may drop
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Viral disease (Begomovirus) transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. No seed transmission in most cases.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment. Control the whitefly vector rigorously. Remove and destroy infected plants early. Use resistant/tolerant varieties. Protect seedlings with insect-proof nets.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance. Balanced nutrition supports plant recovery but does not cure the virus.
prevention: Grow resistant or tolerant tomato varieties
Use insect-proof nets in nursery and early field stages
Control whitefly with yellow sticky traps, neem products and recommended insecticides
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Avoid continuous tomato cropping and manage weeds that host whiteflies

symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves
Leaf distortion, puckering or fern-leaf symptoms
Stunted plants
Fruit may show uneven ripening or internal browning
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Viral disease caused by Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) or related Tobamoviruses. Highly contagious; spreads by mechanical means (hands, tools, clothing) and can be seed-borne.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment. Remove and destroy infected plants. Disinfect tools and hands with soap or trisodium phosphate. Use virus-free seed and resistant varieties.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties
Disinfect tools, hands and stakes regularly
Avoid smoking or handling tobacco near tomato plants (related viruses)
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Control weeds that may harbour the virus
